gaps.title: SLSA provenance cannot be honestly produced by a post-hoc scanner; recorded rather than faked
gaps.problem: The mandatory P0 baseline requires supply-chain standards including SLSA. A scanner cannot satisfy it, and emitting a SLSA provenance statement would be a fabricated attestation.
gaps.reference_tool: SLSA provenance and in-toto attestations; Sigstore/cosign
gaps.how_reference_does_it: The BUILD SYSTEM attests what it built: builder identity, buildType, materials with digests, and it is generated during the build and signed. The attestation is a claim by the producer, not an observer.
gaps.current_behavior: scanner/runtime_artifact_integrity_engine.py already computes component hashes and integrity state for the artefacts it inspects, and reporting/cyclonedx_export.py and reporting/vex_export.py emit machine-readable documents. SLSA is 0 hits; in-toto has a single incidental mention; there is no provenance emitter. V11 runs AFTER the build and is not the builder.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN by design, and this row exists to stop the obvious wrong fix. The tempting implementation - have V11 emit a SLSA-shaped provenance document from the hashes it can see - would be an unsigned, unattested document asserting provenance that no build system ever asserted, i.e. a counterfeit supply-chain attestation. That is worse than the current honest absence. Closing this legitimately requires one of: (a) build-system integration, where the CI pipeline that built the artefacts emits the provenance and V11 only verifies it; (b) an agreed scanner-observation format that is unmistakably labelled as observer output and not a producer attestation, which is a design decision needing consumer agreement; or (c) leaving it unimplemented and declaring it not-applicable in the report. V11's own CycloneDX output already carries a zero_day_status property and integrity data, so the integrity evidence exists; only the attestation authority does not.
gaps.implementation_location: would require either CI/build-pipeline integration outside this repository, or a new reporting/ provenance emitter in scanner/runtime_artifact_integrity_engine.py guarded by an explicit observer-vs-attestation label. Neither is in scope without a consumer decision.
gaps.evidence: analysis/benchmark_conformance_baseline.py SUPPLY_CHAIN: cyclonedx_export PASS, vex_export PASS, spdx_export FAIL, slsa_provenance FAIL; independent greps: SLSA 0 hits, CSAF 0 hits, SPDX 6 vocabulary hits with 0 exporters, in-toto 1 incidental mention

gaps.title: Per-finding decision fields are computed for every finding and rendered in no artifact
gaps.problem: The pipeline records a disposition for every finding -- whether it is reportable, what its decision state is, and whether its evidence validated -- and none of the three appears in the JSON-derived PDF text, either workbook, the SARIF, or the console. A reader therefore cannot tell a finding the pipeline stands behind from one it flagged for review, and cannot tell whether a missing field means 'fine' or 'never recorded'.
gaps.reference_tool: GitHub Advanced Security; Snyk; Bugcrowd triage
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Surfaces the triage disposition next to each finding and refuses to display a finding as clean when no disposition was recorded, rather than leaving the field blank.
gaps.current_behavior: Measured over the 19:14 artifact: decision_state is REVIEW_REQUIRED on 68 of 102 findings and absent on 34; reportable_finding is true on exactly the same 68; evidence_valid is true on 101 and false on 1. None of the three strings appeared anywhere in the rendered Security_Report.pdf, the executive PDF, any of the three workbooks, or the SARIF. Detailed Findings showed File / Line / CWE / OWASP / MITRE / CVE / PCI DSS / NIST / ISO 27001 / SOC 2 / Detection / Sink Category / Confidence / Exploitability -- nothing after the pipeline's own verdict.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The three per-finding disposition fields (decision_state, reportable_finding, evidence_valid) are now rendered in every surface: the technical PDF's per-finding metadata table, the Findings sheet of all three workbooks, and each SARIF result's properties. The absence rule is pinned by tests in every renderer: a missing value renders as NOT_RECORDED and never as a verdict, because None->'not reportable' or None->VALID would convert a missing decision into a claim about the code. In SARIF the values are stringified rather than emitted as booleans so the three states stay distinguishable for automation -- a boolean could only ever express two of them. CYCLEDX IS DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE: CycloneDX 1.x models components and component vulnerabilities, not source findings, so a per-finding disposition has no field. Adding one would mean violating the schema or misusing a property, and the SBOM already carries the evidence that matters there (advisories, CVSS, EPSS, KEV, reachability) as properties.
gaps.implementation_location: reporting/pdf_report.py (_decision_state_display, _reportable_display, _evidence_valid_display + meta_rows); reporting/excel_report.py (_excel_decision_state, _excel_reportable, _excel_evidence_valid + the Findings sheet); reporting/sarif_export.py (_decision_properties)
gaps.evidence: Rendered-PDF verification on the Juice Shop corpus: 'Decision' occurs exactly 102 times (one row per finding), 'REVIEW_REQUIRED' exactly 68, 'Reportable' exactly 102 and 'NOT RECORDED' exactly 68 (34 findings x 2 fields), which matches the JSON ground truth exactly and so confirms the renderer neither drops nor invents rows. gaps.title: ASVS is CC BY-SA 4.0; the requirement text was deliberately not vendored and the share-alike question is open

Redistribution of the ATT&CK dataset raised the same question separately and is already open as G-069.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP ASVS project page; SPDX licence identifiers

The 278 requirement DESCRIPTIONS are not copied; the module records ASVS_LICENSE = 'CC BY-SA 4.0', the canonical ASVS_SOURCE_URL and the enumeration SHA-256, and the report cites the source rather than restating the text.

Deciding this silently would be the same error as deciding G-069 silently, so it is registered instead. Note the consequence of the current choice: the ASVS Mapping sheet and the PDF section show identifiers, section names and evidence classes but not the requirement text, so a reader must consult the canonical source to read a requirement.

gaps.title: Attack-path correlation reported ZERO paths on all 16 corpus projects while the findings carried source-to-sink evidence
gaps.problem: Every current clean_report.json in the prodtest corpus carried attack_paths: 0, including juice-shop, which holds 12 findings with genuine source-to-sink taint paths. The tool therefore appeared to model no attack chains at all.
gaps.reference_tool: Any taint-driven exploit-chain correlator; SARIF result-graph convention
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Derives chains from the same taint evidence that produced the finding, so a reported chain and a reported finding cannot disagree.
gaps.current_behavior: REGRESSION, now fixed. core/attack_graph.py::get_attack_paths read finding['taint_path'], which the pipeline emits as a STRING carrying the chain ('body -> fetch('). The function wrapped any non-list value in a single-element list, so the guard `len(nodes) >= 2` was never satisfied and every path was dropped. reporting/pdf_report.py independently tests for the string form ("->" in str(taint_path)), so both ends of the pipeline agreed the string was normal and only this function disagreed -- which is why the defect survived review.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The string is now split on a real arrow, so T1595-style evidence resolves: re-resolving the SAME 16 artifacts (no rescan, no invented findings) yields 749 attack paths, up from 11. Per project: BenchmarkJava-master 0 -> 639, DVWA-master 0 -> 24, juice-shop-git 0 -> 12, WebGoat-main 0 -> 11, GenAI-Red-Team-Lab-main 0 -> 20, wrongsecrets-master 0 -> 4, LLMForge-main 0 -> 8. Four projects (argip-platform, damn-vulnerable-defi-master, VAmPI-master, web-security-testing-guide-master) correctly stay at 0 because they carry no taint evidence. Precision guards held: every path has >=2 nodes, joins are consistent, and no project produced more paths than it has taint-bearing findings. 709 confirmed / 40 candidate. NEGATIVE guard retained: a bare expression with no arrow is NOT a path, and a chain with an interior gap such as 'a ->  -> b' emits NOTHING rather than collapsing to ['a','b'] -- collapsing would assert a direct a->b edge whose hops were never observed.
gaps.implementation_location: core/attack_graph.py (get_attack_paths); tests/test_v11_attack_path_regression.py (16 tests)

Note the three OLD report directories are NOT comparable -- their paths carry keys (narrative, steps, evidence_type, risk_score) from an earlier pattern-driven implementation that synthesised a chain from vuln_type alone, which is why nodegoat-master-v10-idor-regression reads 3 recorded vs 1 resolvable. gaps.title: BenchmarkJava-master shipped every artifact except both PDFs, and the failure was invisible
gaps.problem: BenchmarkJava-master's report directory contained clean_report.json, three XLSX workbooks, SARIF, VEX, SPDX, CycloneDX and Scan_Performance.json -- and no PDF at all. A reader had no way to tell a report that lost its PDF from one where none was requested.
gaps.reference_tool: Any report generator that fails loudly
gaps.how_reference_does_it: A missing artifact is either written or reported as missing; a successful exit never conceals a lost deliverable.
gaps.current_behavior: TWO DEFECTS. (1) generate_pdf_report raised reportlab LayoutError on BenchmarkJava and main.py swallowed it into a single console line, so the run exited 0. (2) The exception itself had a real cause: reporting/pdf_report.py::_code_safe_paragraph_chunks bounded only the running CHARACTER total across source lines, so a minified or bundled asset -- which is ONE line -- bypassed the 1200-char cap entirely and became a single Paragraph of ~32,000 characters and ~4,300 points against a 665-point frame.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Reproduced against the real 112 MB artifact (1367 findings) before fixing. Every individual line is now bounded, and the pieces are re-GROUPED rather than flattened so ordinary multi-line snippets still render as one Paragraph. Also bounded on the LINE axis: the Code style leads at ~11 points, so 50 one-word lines already measured 550 points and 1200 single-character lines would be ~13,200 points -- the same LayoutError by the other route. Result: Security_Report.pdf builds at 9,714,245 bytes where previously no file existed at all. Separately, exporter failures are now accumulated in _REPORT_EXPORT_FAILURES and printed under a REPORT EXPORT FAILURES heading at the end of the run, so a lost artifact can no longer pass as success.
gaps.implementation_location: reporting/pdf_report.py (_code_safe_paragraph_chunks, _split_oversized_line, _CODE_MAX_LINES); main.py (_REPORT_EXPORT_FAILURES); tests/test_v11_pdf_layout_regression.py (20 tests)
gaps.evidence: Before/after on the same payload. Frame measured from the real LayoutError: 481.23 x 665.48 points. An 80,015-character single minified line now yields 67 paragraphs, tallest 143 points. 200 one-character lines yield 4 paragraphs, tallest 605 points. NEGATIVE checks: an ordinary 3-line snippet and a 50-line snippet each still render as exactly ONE paragraph, so no report's layout changed. A zero-width-space wrapping approach was tried and REMOVED: it does not affect height (a 1200-character token already wraps to 72 points) and it silently attaches invisible U+200B to every code paragraph, so a reader copying evidence out of the PDF would get those characters with it.

gaps.title: First measured accuracy baseline: BenchmarkJava recall 0.5512 file-level / 0.5159 with the declared CWE, with four near-empty categories
gaps.problem: Until now the product had one scored project (juice-shop, recall 0.1121 against 116 prose-declared challenges) and no measurement of false positives at all. G-094 recorded this. There was therefore no defensible claim about what the scanner does and does not find.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP Benchmark; SARIF precision/recall convention
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Scores against a machine-readable oracle carrying both polarities, reports per-category recall, and never folds the precision side into recall.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED against BenchmarkJava-master expectedresults-1.2.csv, the only machine-readable oracle in the corpus with BOTH polarities: 2740 cases, 1415 expected-vulnerable and 1325 expected-benign, each with a declared CWE. Format read, not assumed -- the header line is a PROSE COMMENT ('# test name, category, real vulnerability, cwe, Benchmark version: 1.2, 2016-06-1'), the expected column is named 'real vulnerability' not 'expected', and there are NO line numbers, so the oracle is test-case/file level and claiming line-level accuracy would be false precision.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN, with the first fix applied. Baseline on expectedresults-1.2.csv: 2740 cases, 1415 expected-vulnerable, 1325 expected-benign, each with a declared CWE, 2740/2740 test files present. ORIGINAL: recall 0.5512 file-level and 0.5159 requiring the declared CWE. AFTER the path-traversal fix (G-100): recall 0.6064 and 0.5753. The genuine off-target false-positive count FELL from 32 to 23 (0.0242 -> 0.0174) over the same change. The naive any-finding FPR moved 0.1811 -> 0.2204, which is acceptable and expected: the extra benign-file hits are the oracle-artifact population (safe rewrites that still call the dangerous API), not new false positives -- which is exactly why the three-figure precision breakdown is used instead of one number. PER-CATEGORY AFTER THE FIX: crypto 1.0000, weakrand 1.0000, xpathi 1.0000, ldapi 0.7037, hash 0.6899, pathtraver 0.6692 (was 0.0827), sqli 0.6066, cmdi 0.5317, xss 0.2358, trustbound 0.0964, securecookie 0.0000 (was 0.0000; closed by G-102, not yet re-measured end to end). STILL OPEN: xss at 0.2358 is the largest absolute gap and its two candidate rules were both measured and rejected (G-101); trustbound at 0.0964 is untouched because the benign and vulnerable variants differ only in whether the value was HTML-escaped before session storage, and any pattern separating them would be guesswork that risks manufacturing false positives on the 31 benign cases.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/ Java rule sets (xss, pathtraver, trustbound, sqli, cmdi, hash, securecookie); analysis/ oracle + scoring harness
gaps.evidence: D:\Data\Code test\prodtest\reports\benchmarkjava_oracle.json. 2740/2740 test files present, so no case was skipped for a missing file. Findings indexed by test file: 1020. False-positive mass concentrates in 5 rules: JAVA_J5_XSS 54, JAVA_J5_SQL 41, JAVA_TAINT_SQL_INJECTION 38, JAVA_TAINT_COMMAND_INJECTION 30, JAVA_J5_CMD 24. Per-category recall bars are in the generated report; the headline number alone would misrepresent the tool as uniformly mediocre rather than strong on three categories and blind on one.

gaps.title: No cookie-security rule exists anywhere in the product; 36 declared-vulnerable cases are structurally undetectable
gaps.problem: BenchmarkJava declares 36 securecookie test cases vulnerable (all CWE-614, cookie set without Secure) and the scanner detects 0 of them. The cause is a missing capability, not a weak pattern.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP Benchmark securecookie category; CWE-614 and CWE-1004
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Models cookie misconfiguration as a first-class weakness with its own detection shape.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED: 0 rule identifiers containing 'COOKIE' exist in scanner/ or config/, and 0 references to CWE-614 or CWE-1004 exist anywhere in the product. The scanner has no rule that can detect either weakness.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED by G-102. The missing capability is built: scanner/java_web_servlets.py, a variable-scoped CWE-614 check measuring 36 of 36 declared cases with zero false positives across 31 benign cases. The variable scope is what makes it work -- a method-scoped version scored 0 of 36, because BenchmarkTest00087 hardens one cookie and leaves another at setSecure(false), and the method-level check was masked by the hardened one. gaps.title: The J5 path-traversal sink regex could not match fully-qualified constructors, holding recall at 11 of 133
gaps.problem: BenchmarkJava declared 133 path-traversal cases vulnerable (CWE-22) and the scanner detected 11 -- 0.0827, the second-worst category in the corpus. A one-line regex defect explained almost all of it.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP BenchmarkJava expectedresults-1.2.csv
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Declares per-test-case expected results with a CWE, so a category's recall can be attributed to a specific cause rather than guessed at.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED by a single-character-class fix. The J5 path-traversal sink pattern was `\bnew\s+(?:File|FileInputStream|...)`, which requires the literal `new File(`. Real code -- and every one of the 122 missed cases -- writes `new java.io.File(` and `new java.io.FileInputStream(`, where `java` follows `new ` and the alternation never matches. The same blind spot applied to java.nio.file, so the optional package qualifier was added there too.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Re-scanned BenchmarkJava end to end and re-scored against the oracle: pathtraver 11/133 -> 89/133 (0.0827 -> 0.6692, an eightfold gain). Overall recall 0.5512 -> 0.6064, and recall requiring the declared CWE 0.5159 -> 0.5753. Crucially the genuine off-target false-positive count FELL from 32 to 23 (0.0242 -> 0.0174), so this was not a recall gain bought with noise. The naive any-finding FPR rose 0.1811 -> 0.2204, which is the expected and acceptable direction here: benign cases that still call `java.io.File` on request input are the oracle-artifact population identified earlier, not new false positives.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/java_semantic_j5.py (_J5_SINKS path_traversal entry)
gaps.evidence: Before/after scored by the same harness on 1415 declared-vulnerable and 1325 declared-benign cases: 2740/2740 test files present, so no case was skipped for a missing file. Findings 1367 -> 1571. Attack paths 0 -> 843 as a side effect, since the new findings carry taint paths that core/attack_graph.py now resolves (G-096).

gaps.title: XSS recall is 0.2358 (58 of 246); both candidate rules were measured and NEITHER was shipped
gaps.problem: XSS is the largest absolute recall gap in the corpus: 188 of 246 declared cases undetected. Two rules were written for it, measured, and both were rejected on precision grounds.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP BenchmarkJava expectedresults-1.2.csv
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Carries a declared-benign population, so a detection change can be judged on precision as well as recall. Without negatives this gap would have been closed by shipping a noisy rule.
gaps.current_behavior: DIAGNOSED, NOT FIXED. The existing JAVA_J5_XSS sink pattern already matches `response.getWriter().println(`; what fails is the source side. BenchmarkJava writes `String param = ""; ... if (values != null) param = values[0];` -- the assignment that carries the taint shares a physical line with an `if` guard, and the J5 fixpoint's statement splitter hands the whole guarded statement to `_j5_assignment`, which recovers no left-hand side. Measured: 161 of the 188 missed cases do contain the sink.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN, with a rejected fix recorded so it is not retried blind. Variant A (transitive, method-scoped taint): recall 0.5569, FPR 0.4115 -- it fires on 86 of 209 declared-benign cases. Trading 137 true findings for 86 false ones is not a fix, and shipping it would have improved the headline recall while degrading the tool. Variant B (single-hop taint): recall 0.0000, FPR 0.0000 -- precise only because it is blind, since BenchmarkJava never assigns a variable directly from a request source. Recall 0.0000 is not a pass. NEITHER rule ships. The fix this needs is inside the J5 fixpoint's statement splitting, which is a change to shared taint machinery affecting every Java rule, and that deserves its own scoped change with its own regression run rather than being smuggled in alongside a new pattern.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/java_semantic_j5.py (fixpoint statement splitting; the correct place to fix), NOT a new pattern module
gaps.evidence: Both variants evaluated directly over the oracle's own 246 vulnerable and 209 benign xss files, reporting recall and FPR before any 40-minute rescan. tests/test_v11_java_cookie_security.py::test_the_rejected_xss_rule_is_absent_from_production_source asserts the rejected rule stays out of scanner/ and sast.py, and test_the_rejection_is_documented_with_its_numbers pins 0.4115 and 0.0000 on record so the numbers cannot be quietly deleted.

gaps.title: No cookie-security rule existed anywhere; the capability is now built and measures 36 of 36 with zero false positives
gaps.problem: The product had zero rule ids containing COOKIE and zero references to CWE-614 or CWE-1004. BenchmarkJava declares 36 cookie-flag cases vulnerable and the scanner detected none, because nothing could.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP BenchmarkJava securecookie category; CWE-614, CWE-1004
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Models cookie misconfiguration as its own weakness with a distinct detection shape.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. scanner/java_web_servlets.py implements a VARIABLE-SCOPED check: a cookie is reported when its own variable is explicitly set with `setSecure(false)`, or reaches `response.addCookie` with no `setSecure(true)` on that variable. The variable scope is load-bearing and was arrived at by measurement -- a method-scoped version found 0 of 36, because BenchmarkTest00087 hardens one cookie (`userCookie.setSecure(true)`) while leaving a second at `setSecure(false)`, and the method-level check saw the hardened one and suppressed the finding.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Recall 36/36 (1.0000) with 0 false positives across the 31 declared-benign cases. The rule asserts only that the Secure flag is not set on that variable in that method, and says so in the finding's own note: it does NOT claim the cookie reaches a browser over an insecure channel, which a source scan cannot establish. Severity and confidence are both MEDIUM for that reason. Also fixed a real parser defect found while testing it: the method pattern required an access modifier, so a package-private or plain `void f(){}` parsed as no method at all.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/java_web_servlets.py; wired in scanner/sast.py alongside the J5 dedup; tests/test_v11_java_cookie_security.py (26 tests)
gaps.evidence: Scored by tests/test_v11_java_cookie_security.py::test_real_declared_vulnerable_cookie_cases_are_detected, which reads expectedresults-1.2.csv rather than grepping filenames -- an earlier version filtered on `"securecookie" in text`, which also matches the 31 benign cases, correctly did not fire on them, and reported a misleading 3/5. Negative tests cover: a hardened cookie is not reported, HttpOnly alone does not suppress (only Secure is asserted), a cookie never added to a response is not reported, and hardening on a DIFFERENT variable does not mask this one.

gaps.title: A local-path requirement line aborted the entire scan with rc=1 and no artifact at all
gaps.problem: autogen-main could not be scanned. `_parse_requirements` dereferenced a regex match OUTSIDE its `if m:` guard, so any requirement line that is not a package name raised AttributeError, which propagated out of `generate_sbom` and killed the whole run.
gaps.reference_tool: pip requirement syntax; fail-open scanning discipline
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Treats every line of every manifest as data to be recorded, never as a reason to abandon the scan.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Four requirements files in autogen-main contain `/autogen_python/packages/autogen-core`, an editable local install of a sibling package. That is a legitimate pip requirement and it fails the package-name regex. Result: rc=1, no clean_report.json, the project looked unscannable rather than merely imperfect.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED, but the first fix was incomplete and that mattered. The obvious repair -- move the append inside the guard and skip unmatched lines -- stops the crash while dropping the line. A dropped SBOM entry is indistinguishable downstream from an absent dependency, so 12 declared dependencies would have vanished while the scan reported success. The local-reference regex was then wrong too: the compressed pattern `[/~.]{1,2}[/\\]` cannot match an ABSOLUTE POSIX path, because it needs a separator immediately after one-or-two of `/~.` and the next character in `/autogen_python/` is `a`. Final state: the forms are enumerated separately (absolute, ~/, ./, ../, bare ., Windows drive, VCS URL, file:// and https://), local references are RECORDED with version `unknown` and ecosystem `local` -- not `PyPI`, because claiming a PyPI identity for a filesystem path fabricates a package that does not exist -- and each line is handled in its own try/except so no future malformation can abort a scan. Verified: 8/8 autogen requirements files parse, 0 crashes, 28 packages recorded, 12 local references kept, 0 skipped. autogen now scans at rc=0 with 232 findings and 10 attack paths.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/sbom.py (_parse_requirements, _LOCAL_REQUIREMENT_RE, requirements_unparsed_count); tests/test_v11_sbom_requirements_and_wstg.py
gaps.evidence: Reproduced per-file before fixing: four autogen requirements files raised AttributeError at the named local-path line. After the fix, 0 crashes across all 8 files. tests/test_v11_sbom_requirements_and_wstg.py includes test_every_autogen_requirements_file_parses_without_raising against the live corpus and test_a_local_reference_is_recorded_not_dropped, which requires the entry to exist rather than merely not crash.

gaps.title: OWASP WSTG had no traceability at all; v4.2 is now mapped with its scope stated honestly
gaps.problem: WSTG was the second of two remaining mandatory P0 standards with no implementation. Mapping to it naively would have been misleading, because WSTG is a TESTING guide.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide v4.2
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Defines procedures a tester performs against a running application.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. core/wstg_mappings.py, GENERATED and pinned. 97 test cases across 12 categories, catalogue digest (SHA-256 over id|title|file) 29E453B1EE9C2CE5256A78EC60E375A3982C9B8569B6034E262DF50F94033841, 51 rules mapped. Ids were parsed from each section page's `|WSTG-XXX-NN|` row; the structured `_data/v42.yaml` is a table of contents carrying no ids, so it is not the source. 72 of 97 cases are in statically-attestable categories and 25 are not.

A WSTG mapping does NOT mean the test was performed -- the tool performs static source analysis, and most WSTG cases need a running application (log in as another user, time a response, walk a workflow, test subdomain takeover). That distinction is enforced as data rather than prose: every test case carries `static_attestable`, and the 25 cases a source scan cannot discharge are listed with the reason in WSTG_NOT_STATIC_ATTESTABLE rather than counted as covered. LICENCE RECORDED AS UNVERIFIED, deliberately: the checkout has no root LICENSE file, so unlike ASVS (CC BY-SA, G-092) and SANS (CC BY 4.0) no terms could be read and none is asserted. gaps.title: Attack paths were published with empty chains, a fabricated 'Risk: 0', and every confirmed path labelled PATTERN-ONLY; the executive report omitted them entirely
gaps.problem: The Attack Path Correlation chapter existed and correctly stated the COUNT ('the following 8 attack paths were identified'), so the section looked populated. The CONTENT was empty and the evidence label was wrong.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP Benchmark-style report accuracy; SARIF result-graph convention
gaps.how_reference_does_it: A reported chain must carry its observed nodes and its real evidence state. A document that states the right number and the wrong content is worse than one that is silent, because it looks authoritative.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Reproduced against babyagi-main's own artifact: all eight paths are `attack_path_status: confirmed` with real nodes, e.g. `['route parameter {function_name}', 'function_name', 'g.functionz.executor.execute']`. The rendered PDF showed, for every one: `Chain #01  MEDIUM  Risk: 0`, then `Chain:` followed by nothing, then "PATTERN-ONLY - Candidate attack path. Manual validation is required". THREE wrongnesses, one cause -- the renderers read the LEGACY record shape (`steps`, `risk_score`, `evidence_type`, `chains_to`) that core/attack_graph.py stopped emitting, and formatted the defaults: empty Chain from `steps` defaulting to []; 'Risk: 0' from `risk_score` defaulting to 0, a formatted default that reads like a measurement; and PATTERN-ONLY from `evidence_type` defaulting to 'pattern-detected'. The executive PDF had NO attack-path content whatsoever, so the document a decision-maker reads showed nothing at all. The workbook's Attack Paths sheet had the same defect: blank Entry Point / Exploit / Pivot / Impact cells in all three workbooks.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED, then partially REGRESSED and re-closed. The original fix corrected the evidence label and the chain but stripped three elements the report genuinely had -- the Risk column, the narrative and the human-readable title -- because it read a field the producer had never emitted and reported it as absent. That regression is tracked separately as G-108, because it has a different cause (a producer that never propagated the finding's own fields) and a different fix. Both are closed; G-106 covers the record-shape contract and reporting/attack_path_view.py as the single source of truth, G-108 covers the content the producer was failing to carry.
gaps.implementation_location: reporting/attack_path_view.py (new, single source of truth); reporting/pdf_report.py (_attack_paths_section); reporting/excel_report.py (_attack_paths); reporting/executive_pdf_report.py (_executive_attack_path_summary); tests/test_v11_attack_path_publication.py (26 tests)
gaps.evidence: All three outputs regenerated from the SAME stored artifact, so any difference is the renderer's doing: technical PDF 10/10 distinct chain nodes rendered, 9 CONFIRMED labels, 0 PATTERN-ONLY, 0 'Risk: 0'; executive PDF shows the section, the count, the confirmed/candidate split, the originating rule and 9/10 nodes, and states that live exploitability is a separate question; all three workbooks carry CONFIRMED labels, a Record Shape value and 10/10 nodes in the technical sheet. Reports were re-rendered rather than rescanned, which is what makes the attribution clean: the renderer change cannot be confused with a change in findings.

gaps.title: Rendered PDFs contained mojibake; the artifact was clean, so the corruption was introduced in the renderer
gaps.problem: Security_Report.pdf and Security_Executive_Report.pdf each carried a corrupt token three times, in the top-root-causes remediation note. A reader saw garbage where a remediation statement should be.
gaps.reference_tool: Unicode encoding discipline; cp1252/UTF-8 round-trip diagnostics
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Text entering a report is decoded once and rendered once, and the rendered artifact is checked for replacement characters before delivery.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Three layers were independently wrong. (1) SOURCE: 63 occurrences across 7 files. The one that reached the PDF was a literal in reporting/pdf_report.py. (2) THE CLEANER: `clean_mojibake` was a 9-entry lookup table covering only single-round-trip forms, so it could not have fixed this token -- and it was imported by pdf_report.py and excel_report.py while being called ZERO times. (3) NOTHING AT THE RENDER BOUNDARY to catch anything arriving from a manifest, a finding, or a dependency name that has travelled an unknown number of encodings.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The corrupt token was unravalled by decoding rather than by guessing: it is U+2726 BLACK FOUR POINTED STAR, a decorative list marker, triple-encoded (UTF-8 bytes decoded as cp1252 and re-encoded as UTF-8, three times). Substituted with an ASCII hyphen, which is correct on two axes -- U+2726 is not in the standard PDF Type1 repertoire, so even correctly encoded it would not render in Helvetica. clean_mojibake is now an ITERATIVE, SCORED decoder: it round-trips until stable and accepts a result only if the mojibake signature count STRICTLY drops. That acceptance test is the safety property and it is asserted directly: 'cafe', CJK filenames and Cyrillic come back byte-identical, so the cleaner cannot corrupt a legitimate name in an inventory. The cleaner is now actually invoked in _paragraph_chunks, the central prose path. gaps.title: CERT-In Quantum Bill of Materials was absent; a Table 8 layer is now emitted as a separate artifact
gaps.problem: CERT-In v2.0 was the last NOT_VERIFIED mandatory standard. Its QBOM layer did not exist, and the probe resolved payload['qbom'], which nothing wrote.
gaps.reference_tool: CERT-In Technical Guidelines on SBOM, QBOM & CBOM, AIBOM and HBOM v2.0, Table 8
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Prescribes 11 minimum elements per BOM type and expects each BOM to be a distinct artifact with its own vocabulary.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED, PARTIAL BY CONSTRUCTION. core/qbom_mappings.py implements Table 8 and main.py emits Security_QBOM.qbom.json alongside -- and separately from -- the SBOM, because CERT-In defines SBOM/QBOM/CBOM/AIBOM/HBOM as distinct types with distinct element tables, and folding QBOM into the SBOM would erase which table a field came from. All 11 element names were verified present in the pinned PDF (SHA-256 28AA48F...FF5151, 66 pages), so the transcription is checked rather than asserted. All three QBOM probes pass. CERT_IN remains NOT_VERIFIED because HBOM (Table 11), the AIBOM Table 10 minimum elements and CSAF are still outstanding.
gaps.actual_gap: PARTIAL BY CONSTRUCTION, and that limit is structural rather than oversight. This is a static source analyser: it can see the SBOM, the findings and the advisories, but it cannot see a quantum device in a datacentre. So of the 11 Table 8 elements, 5 are observable from source (License Information, Cryptographic Asset, Software Dependencies, Vulnerabilities Information, Attestations) and 6 describe physical hardware (Model Name, Version, Vendor & Origin, Communication Protocol, Hardware, Environmental Impact). The 6 are emitted as null carrying NOT_OBSERVABLE_FROM_SOURCE and a stated reason, so partial coverage is visible to a consumer rather than implied by a document that looks complete. NOTHING IS INVENTED: quantum components are listed only when a resolved SBOM name matches a known quantum SDK, and on babyagi-main -- a plain Python task-runner -- the list is EMPTY with quantum_components_detected false. An empty inventory that says it is empty is the truthful output; a populated one would be fabrication. The Attestations element is a SHA-256 content digest and says so: it is not a digital signature, because no signing key is held, so the element's authenticity guarantee is only partially satisfied and the artifact records that.

gaps.evidence: Single-target end-to-end scan of babyagi-main: 20 findings, 8 attack paths, Security_QBOM.qbom.json 13.1 KB, rc=0. The Table 8 digest was independently recomputed from the pinned PDF rather than transcribed from memory. TWO DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED EN ROUTE, both by asserting on output rather than on code. First, the attestation digest stripped the `value` key from EVERY element before hashing, so it covered element names and statuses and none of the inventory: every value could be altered and the attestation would not move. An attestation that does not detect modification of what it attests to is decoration. Second, the emitter wrote qbom_summary only, so the document was on disk but unreachable at payload['qbom'] -- the path the probe resolves -- and the probe correctly reported `path 'qbom' unresolved`. gaps.title: External advisory lookup failed CLOSED on a non-JSON 200 response, aborting the whole scan intermittently
gaps.problem: scanner/vulnerability_intel.py guarded its OSV call with `except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError, OSError)`. An intermediary answering HTTP 200 with an HTML body (corporate proxy, captive portal, rate limiter) raises nothing from urlopen, and json.loads then raises JSONDecodeError -- a subclass of ValueError, not OSError -- so it escaped the handler entirely.
gaps.reference_tool: Any HTTP client: a non-2xx is a transport error, a 2xx with an unexpected body is a contract error, and the two need different handling.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Parse and shape-validate the payload, raise a typed error, and fail open with the degradation recorded.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. The exception propagated out of query_osv_batch, out of enrich_packages_with_external_vulns, out of generate_sbom and aborted the scan. Observed on prodtest AI Benchmarks autogen-main as an intermittent rc=1 with no artifact; the identical re-run gave rc=0 and 232 findings, so the failure was transient and therefore indistinguishable from a scan that never ran. A JSON array instead of an object was equally fatal via `data.get` -> AttributeError.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Added `AdvisoryServiceUnavailable` and `_decode_json_object`, which validates both parseability and that the result is an object; broadened the batch guard to include it and to tolerate a non-list `results`; guarded the enrich call site in scanner/sbom.py so an unanticipated enrichment failure cannot take the SBOM down with it. Fails OPEN: the scan completes. The dangerous outcome was never the crash but the silent version -- an empty advisory result makes every package look CVE-free, so ADVISORY_SERVICE_STATUS and `advisory_service_status()` record availability, batch counts and a per-batch failure reason, and main.py writes payload['sbom_advisory_status'] plus a WARNING line so a report can say 'no known vulnerabilities' and 'we could not ask' apart. CLASSIFICATION CAVEAT: no class in the controlled vocabulary covers 'an external dependency's unavailability aborted the pipeline'. DATA_GAP is the nearest available class and is not fully accurate -- DATA_GAP means intelligence is a static placeholder rather than a live feed, whereas here the feed was live and unreachable. The class is extended rather than a new one invented, so the grouping stays analysable; the precise wording lives in this row.

gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The element now carries the classified asset inventory: usage sites, distinct assets, classification coverage, per-status counts, the migration queue, and per-asset algorithm / normalized form / provenance / key size / occurrence count / quantum status / risk / priority / caveat / confidence, ordered most-exposed-first. Table 9's per-asset fields remain in the CBOM artifact and the element says so, since the two are different tables. When no CBOM exists the element returns an observed-and-empty value rather than null, because null in this schema means 'not observable from source' and collapsing 'we looked and found no cryptography' into 'we cannot tell' is how an inventory manufactures false assurance. test_observable_elements_actually_carry_values caught the None variant immediately.
gaps.implementation_location: core/qbom_mappings.py (_cryptographic_asset_element, build_qbom)
gaps.evidence: Read from real artifacts, not asserted from code: BenchmarkJava-master now reports 3111 usage sites, 4 distinct assets, by_quantum_status {UNKNOWN: 3, QUANTUM_VULNERABLE: 1}, 1 migration-queue entry. Verified on 19 artifacts with a CBOM. tests/test_v11_entrypoint_smoke.py::test_table8_cryptographic_asset_carries_data_not_a_pointer asserts the element is a populated object and that 'reference' is absent, which is the old shape.

gaps.title: Name collision returned a set where a status string was expected, failing two frames from the cause
gaps.problem: resolve_symmetric_family returned the module-level SET `QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED` -- the collection of hash and cipher names -- where the status string of the same name was intended.
gaps.reference_tool: Same name, two different things, distinguished only by type.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: One name per concept; where a legacy name must be kept, the collision is explicit.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. classify_quantum_status('AES') returned a set. Two frames later the risk-mapping lookup `risk_map[quantum_status]` raised `TypeError: cannot use 'set' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'set')`, and the traceback pointed at the dict literal rather than at the function that produced the set. Invisible to review, invisible to the compile gate, and only reachable by actually classifying a bare symmetric name.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The status is now a string literal with the collision documented in place. Added test_status_values_are_all_strings, which asserts every classification is a str and is one of the five known status values -- a type assertion rather than a value assertion, so a future regression of this class fails whatever the values happen to be. The long-term fix would be renaming the set, but that is an API change to a name other code may import; recorded rather than taken unilaterally.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/qbom_model.py (resolve_symmetric_family)
gaps.evidence: Reproduced directly: classify_quantum_status('AES') returned {'aes-128','sha-224',...} with type 'set'. After the fix: 'QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED' with type 'str'. Guarded by test_status_values_are_all_strings across AES, DES, RSA, ML-KEM, MD5, TLS / SSL and 3DES.

gaps.title: A bare symmetric family name was reported UNKNOWN, which asserts we cannot classify it at all
gaps.problem: The classifier had no rule for a family name carrying no key size. 'AES' (93 real occurrences) and 'DES / 3DES' (3,011) therefore fell through to UNKNOWN.
gaps.reference_tool: Grover's algorithm reduces an n-bit key to roughly n/2 bits of effective security.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Separate 'is the primitive broken' from 'how much margin is left'. The first is answerable from the family name; only the second needs the size.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Reporting bare AES as UNKNOWN asserted we cannot place it on the broken-or-not axis, which is false -- Grover-reducible is knowable from the family alone, and only the magnitude depends on the size. Reporting 'DES / 3DES' as UNKNOWN was worse: the single largest class in the corpus was classified as unassessable rather than as the obsolete primitive it is.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED, and the axis separation is the substance. AES with no recorded size -> QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED with classification_note stating that the residual margin cannot be quantified; the caveat travels on the asset because 'not broken' and 'not broken by enough' are different claims and a verdict without its caveat overstates it. AES-256 needs no caveat because the parameterised name already encodes its size. DES and 3DES get a NEW status, QUANTUM_MARGIN_CRITICAL, rather than being folded into QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED: their 64-bit key falls to about 32 bits under Grover, below any acceptable floor, and 3DES was retired by NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 independently of quantum computing. It is separate from QUANTUM_VULNERABLE because the mechanism is not Shor's and the advice differs -- an asymmetric primitive must be replaced, a 64-bit symmetric key must simply be replaced by one of adequate length. Overloading one label with both mechanisms would produce one piece of advice for two different problems.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/qbom_model.py (GROVER_REDUCIBLE_FAMILIES, GROVER_DESTROYED_FAMILIES, resolve_symmetric_family, classification_note, QUANTUM_MARGIN_CRITICAL); scanner/crypto_quantum_analyzer.py; core/qbom_mappings.py; main.py (classification_rules)
gaps.evidence: The 8 distinct component values in the corpus, before and after. Before: DES / 3DES UNKNOWN, AES UNKNOWN, SHA1 UNKNOWN, TLS / SSL UNKNOWN, MD5 UNKNOWN, RC4 UNKNOWN, RSA QUANTUM_VULNERABLE, Hardcoded Private Key UNKNOWN -- 1 of 8 resolved. After: DES / 3DES QUANTUM_MARGIN_CRITICAL (risk HIGH, priority MEDIUM), AES QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED with caveat, SHA1 QUANTUM_IMPACT_ASSESSED, RSA QUANTUM_VULNERABLE, TLS / SSL / MD5 / RC4 UNKNOWN (deliberately: no primitive with a quantum role), Hardcoded Private Key filtered as not-a-primitive. Tests: test_bare_aes_is_classified_without_a_key_size, test_bare_aes_states_that_the_margin_is_unquantifiable, test_parameterised_aes_needs_no_caveat, test_des_is_margin_critical_not_shor_broken, test_the_corpus_largest_class_is_no_longer_unknown, test_margin_critical_assets_reach_the_migration_queue, test_non_primitives_are_left_unclassified.

gaps.title: Both QBOM layers existed as artifacts and appeared in NO human-readable report
gaps.problem: The QBOM documents were written to disk and attached to the payload, and the reporting layer contained zero references to either. A grep for 'qbom' across reporting/ returned 0 matches.
gaps.reference_tool: A capability that exists as a JSON file and appears in no report is not delivered.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Every artifact layer gets a section or sheet, with the content assertions made against rendered output.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. The CERT-In Table 8 conformance document and the PQ exposure layer were both invisible in every PDF and every workbook while the scan exited 0 and every artifact looked complete. This is the AGENTS.md reporting pitfall in its most consequential form: a change can compile, run, write a plausible artifact, and have no observable effect on what a reader sees. The layer existed; the delivery did not.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Added _pq_qbom_section() to reporting/pdf_report.py as its own numbered section in the technical report, and _qbom_pq() to reporting/excel_report.py as a 'PQ QBOM' sheet in ALL THREE workbooks -- technical, standard and executive. The executive workbook omits the other BOM layers by design, so carrying PQ QBOM there is a deliberate exception and is asserted as such: post-quantum exposure is a migration programme with a cost and a horizon, and an executive not shown that a Shor-broken primitive is deployed cannot fund the migration. The sheet leads with coverage rather than with rows, so it reads as a summary in the executive context. Each rendering states which assets break and by which mechanism, discloses what could not be classified and marks UNKNOWN explicitly as not a safe result, declares the usage-site-to-asset aggregation, and records absent key sizes as 'not recorded' rather than inventing a value.
gaps.implementation_location: reporting/pdf_report.py (_pq_qbom_section, registered in the technical story); reporting/excel_report.py (_qbom_pq, wired into all three workbook builders); tests/test_v11_pq_qbom_reporting.py
gaps.evidence: Before: grep for 'qbom' across reporting/*.py returned 0 matches. After: 13 tests in tests/test_v11_pq_qbom_reporting.py assert against the RENDERED artefacts -- pypdf text extraction for the PDF and openpyxl cell reads for the workbooks -- not against source. End to end on prodtest wrongsecrets-master with all reports enabled (RC=0): Security_Report.pdf 1,177,900 bytes contains the section, the algorithm RSA, QUANTUM_VULNERABLE, and the aggregation declaration; all three workbooks carry a populated 'PQ QBOM' sheet. NOTE ON A FAILED VERIFIER: the first version of this check failed all 22 content assertions while the sheets were demonstrably correct -- a regex over raw PDF bytes cannot read compressed content streams, and parsing xl/sharedStrings.xml misses cells openpyxl writes inline. Rewritten with the libraries that produced the files. A test that reports a defect which is not there is worse than no test, because the next reader cannot tell it apart from a real one.

gaps.title: QBOM documents were built AFTER the PDF was generated, so the PDF contradicted the report it came from
gaps.problem: payload['qbom'] was assigned at main.py:4776 and payload['qbom_pq'] at main.py:4893, while generate_pdf_report() ran at main.py:4710 -- both assignments after the PDF had already been rendered.
gaps.reference_tool: A report and its own data source must not disagree.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Compute the payload completely, then render. Artifacts are downstream of the payload, never beside it.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. The PDF's post-quantum section rendered 'No post-quantum exposure assessment was produced for this scan. That is not a statement that the project is post-quantum ready' on a run whose clean_report.json carried a fully populated PQ layer. Two artifacts of one scan disagreed about whether the scan had an assessment, and nothing surfaced the disagreement: the run exited 0 and both files existed. This is the AGENTS.md hazard that report aggregates go stale, in its most literal form.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Both documents are now computed in _build_qbom_layers(payload), called while the payload is still being assembled, and the late report stage only serialises them to disk. Each layer fails open independently: a document that cannot be built is recorded as REVIEW_REQUIRED with its reason in payload['qbom_summary'] / payload['qbom_pq_summary'] and in _REPORT_EXPORT_FAILURES, because losing an entire report to one BOM type would trade a disclosed gap for a silent one. The late block now performs no computation -- verified by asserting the old compute-time imports occur zero times.
gaps.implementation_location: main.py (_build_qbom_layers, called after payload['cbom'] is set; the report stage reduced to serialisation)
gaps.evidence: Measured line positions before the fix: generate_pdf_report at 4710, payload['qbom'] = at 4776, payload['qbom_pq'] = at 4893. Observed failure text quoted from the extracted PDF of a real RC=0 scan. After the fix the same scan's PDF contains the section, the algorithm, a quantum status and the aggregation. Verified structurally: 'build_qbom as _build_qbom' and 'correlate_cbom_to_qbom as _correlate' now occur 0 times in main.py, _build_qbom_layers is defined once and its result written once. End-to-end verified by a standalone script reading the real artifacts.

gaps.title: The corpus harness timeout was not enforced; each timed-out project cost its budget plus a 55-minute kill failure
gaps.problem: The sweep reported `rc=-9 after 10519s  TIMEOUT after 7200s` for llama_index-main. subprocess.run kills only the direct child; the scanner builds a process pool, and those grandchildren hold the stdout/stderr pipe open, so communicate() blocks long after the kill is issued.
gaps.reference_tool: A timeout that overshoots by 46% is not a timeout.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Kill the process tree, not the process. taskkill /T /F on Windows, process groups elsewhere.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Two of nine projects looked like 'slow' when what had actually happened was 'the harness cannot stop them', and every retry paid the overshoot on top of the budget. Raising the timeout -- the obvious response -- would have made each subsequent run slower and taught nothing, because the cost was in the kill, not in the scan.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. scan_one rewritten around Popen with an explicit _kill_tree() that terminates the process TREE (taskkill /T /F on Windows, os.killpg on POSIX) before reading the pipes, plus a bounded second communicate so a survivor cannot block the harness indefinitely. Verified with a test that spawns a child which spawns a grandchild holding the same pipe, waits for the grandchild to announce itself so the race cannot be lost, then asserts the pipe closes within 20s of the kill. The test exists because the original defect was invisible: it only manifested as a slow timeout, which reads as a slow project.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (_kill_tree, scan_one); tests/test_v11_bench_runner.py
gaps.evidence: Observed: 10,519s wall for a 7,200s budget. 23 tests in tests/test_v11_bench_runner.py, including test_kill_tree_terminates_a_process_that_spawned_a_grandchild, which asserts the stdout pipe is readable within 20s after the kill and fails with an explicit message naming the surviving grandchild.

gaps.title: A timeout discarded the output it was holding, and the phase-timing parser shipped matching nothing
gaps.problem: Two defects in one diagnostic. The TimeoutExpired handler set tail="", discarding the captured output the exception carries. And the ELAPSED parser assumed a `\d+h:\d+m:\d+s` format with literal separators, while main.py's _format_duration emits MM:SS.ss under an hour and HH:MM:SS.ss at or above.
gaps.reference_tool: A timeout must say WHERE it was when it ran out.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Retain TimeoutExpired.stdout/stderr, and parse the producer's real format rather than an assumed one.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. A timeout produced no evidence about whether the scan was hung or merely slow -- opposite problems with opposite fixes -- so the only available response was to raise the timeout. The parser was worse: it compiled, ran, and returned an empty list, which is indistinguishable from 'this scan recorded no phases'. Every phase-timing field would have been empty forever, silently. A diagnostic that is present, plausible and empty is worse than one that is absent, because it is believed.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Output captured before the deadline is retained and stored on the entry, including an explicit marker when the capture itself was incomplete. Phase timings are parsed from real PHASE END lines and stored per project, longest first, together with the phase that had started but never finished -- the one field that turns 'TIMEOUT' into 'stalled in Scanning codebase'. The duration token is split structurally so both formats parse; a backdated-fixture test asserts an exact 1.22s phase is reported as 1.22 and not rounded to 1.2, since _format_duration emits two decimals and a diagnostic that rounds away the precision it is reporting is reporting a different number than the scanner printed.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (parse_phase_timings, parse_last_started_phase, _duration_seconds, scan_one); tests/test_v11_bench_runner.py
gaps.evidence: The silent-no-op was caught by asserting the parser against REAL captured scanner output rather than a hand-written sample -- which is exactly how the broken regex came to look correct. First run of that assertion: 6 of 13 checks failed, the parser returning an empty list on genuine text. Fixed to split on ':' and handle both arities. Now 23 tests pass, including both duration shapes (00:05.40 -> 5.4, 01:23:45.67 -> 5025.67), garbage tokens returning None rather than raising, and parse_last_started_phase naming the in-flight phase at a truncation point.

gaps.title: AI-corpus artifacts all predated the current build; transformers-main is now rescanned and quotable, llama_index-main has no artifact
gaps.problem: The harness re-derived any existing clean_report.json without checking whether it still reflected the code that produced it, and counted it in the 'projects scanned cleanly' tally with returncode 0.
gaps.reference_tool: A corpus number describes the build that produced it. G-091 already recorded one instance of this at the artifact level.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Compare the artifact against the newest production source and refuse to present an older artifact as a current result.
gaps.current_behavior: SUBSTANTIALLY CLOSED. transformers-main has been rescanned against the current build and now completes within budget: 4,174 findings over 1,788 kloc, 36 rules, rc=0, no staleness flag. The corpus is now 2 of 9 describing the current build (babyagi-main and transformers-main), 6 reporting a stale artifact on their own line and excluded from the totals, and 1 -- llama_index-main -- with NO artifact at all after its stale artifact was deleted for the bounded diagnostic and never regenerated. Totals over the current build: 4,193 findings over 1,795 kloc.
gaps.actual_gap: SUBSTANTIALLY CLOSED, WITH ONE PROJECT STILL MISSING. Staleness detection was already closed and is now demonstrated on the project that was previously the worst case: transformers-main went from never completing at any budget tried (5,400s, 7,200s twice) to completing, once G-134 removed the OWASP LLM engine's bottleneck. That is the causal chain measured end to end, not asserted: phase 1,648.0s -> 599.0s, and the run moved from stalling mid-scan to stalling in the final PDF phase, which then completed under a larger budget. STILL OPEN: llama_index-main has no artifact. Its 900s diagnostic showed the same rule engine as the dominant cost there -- OWASP LLM 217.5s against a 95.4s codebase scan, 3.02x the AI-BOM and ML-BOM layers combined at 289s -- plus an 'Exposure surface intelligence' phase that started and did not finish inside the budget, so there may be a second stall distinct from the one fixed. Deleting an artifact in order to measure it traded a quotable-but-stale row for an absent one, which is the correct trade for measurement but must not be left as the final state.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (newest_production_source_mtime, artifact_staleness, _modules_newer_than, main); tests/test_v11_corpus_freshness.py
gaps.evidence: Measured staleness for all nine artifacts with the age and the modules responsible: transformers 0.8h, semantic-kernel 2.2h, llama_index 3.2h, autogen 4.5h, diffusers 5.1h, AgentGPT/babyagi/peft/Open-Assistant each older still, with scanner/qbom_model.py, scanner/crypto_quantum_analyzer.py, scanner/sbom.py, scanner/vulnerability_intel.py, core/qbom_mappings.py and main.py named as changed since. Sweep output after the fix: 'projects scanned cleanly : 0 / 9', 'from a stale artifact : 9', '[stale] findings : 11115 over 4268 kloc -- EXCLUDED from the totals above'. DESIGN NOTE: the test suite deliberately does NOT assert that the corpus is fresh. A rescan costs hours and the corpus is external state, so such a test would leave the suite permanently red for an already-disclosed condition; a gate that always fails teaches people to ignore it. The tests assert that the DETECTOR is correct and that whatever is accepted as current is complete.

gaps.title: Attack paths published raw scanner-host absolute paths and a doubled directory component
gaps.problem: core/attack_graph.py built each path's `file` from the finding's PRE-normalisation value, and main.py's _normalize_finding_paths only ever walked `findings`. Attack paths were therefore never normalised.
gaps.reference_tool: AGENTS.md hazard: the report must not disclose the scanner host's filesystem layout.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Every location-bearing record gets the same path treatment, and prose that embeds a path is rewritten with it.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. On prodtest AI Benchmarks babyagi-main, 8 of 8 attack paths carried 'D:\Data\Code test\prodtest\AI Benchmarks\babyagi-main\babyagi-main\babyagi\api\__init__.py' while all 285 findings carried 'babyagi/api/__init__.py'. Two defects in one string: the scanner host's absolute layout is disclosed (G-070, still open), and the project directory is DOUBLED because the corpus nests AI Benchmarks/<project>/<project>. The rendered narrative read 'Observed at D:\...\babyagi-main\babyagi-main\...' -- a path no reader can open, and not the path the findings table shows for the same defect.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. _normalize_attack_path_paths() applies to_report_path to every attack path, and rewrites the narrative's embedded path so the prose and the field cannot disagree. The same render also fixed two further defects reported from that screenshot: scanner/taint_engine.py labelled a route-parameter source as 'route parameter {function_name}', where the braces made a rendered narrative read as an unfilled template placeholder rather than as code (the real variable is function_name); and because the doubled path was the only thing distinguishing two SQL-injection call sites at __init__.py:68 and :71, identical titles were indistinguishable until the paths became relative. reporting/attack_path_view.py additionally strips the brace form so the three corpus directories holding pre-fix artifacts read correctly too, on a copy so the artifact is not mutated.
gaps.implementation_location: main.py (_normalize_attack_path_paths); scanner/taint_engine.py (route parameter label); reporting/attack_path_view.py (_strip_route_param_braces)
gaps.evidence: Before: 8 of 8 attack paths carried the absolute doubled path, 0 findings did. After a full rescan of babyagi-main: absolute host paths remaining in attack_paths = 0, doubled components remaining = 0, occurrences of 'route parameter {' in the artifact = 0, and the narrative now reads '... traces from route parameter function_name to g.functionz.executor.execute across 2 hops ... Observed at babyagi/api/__init__.py:68.' The two SQL-injection paths are now distinguished by :68 and :71. 3 new tests in tests/test_v11_attack_path_publication.py cover the brace strip, the untouched non-placeholder nodes, and non-mutation of the input record.

gaps.title: 98.6% of the package list reported a vulnerability-age measurement gap where no measurement was due
gaps.problem: analysis/vulnerability_age_engine.py derived vulnerability_age_bucket from age_days alone, and None mapped to UNKNOWN. A package with no advisory also has no age_days, so it was labelled UNKNOWN -- asserting we looked and could not date it.
gaps.reference_tool: Vulnerability age is a property of a disclosure. With no disclosure the field does not apply.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Distinguish 'no advisory exists' from 'an advisory we could not date'.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Measured on prodtest/wrongsecrets-master: 691 of 701 packages carry no CVE or advisory, and all 691 were labelled UNKNOWN with vulnerability_age_days None. 98.6% of the list claiming a measurement gap, which buries the ten packages that do have a dated disclosure and gives a compliance reader a false impression that the scan could not see most of the estate.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. _age_bucket takes has_disclosure and returns NOT_APPLICABLE when there is no advisory and UNKNOWN only when an advisory exists but could not be dated; both call sites pass bool(cve), and the human-readable vulnerability_age now says 'Not applicable' rather than 'Unknown' on the same condition. The distinction is not cosmetic: 'we cannot date this' is a reason to go and find out, 'there is nothing here' is a reason to stop.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/vulnerability_age_engine.py (_age_bucket and both call sites)
gaps.evidence: Before: vulnerability_age_bucket distribution on wrongsecrets-master was {UNKNOWN: 691, RECENT: 3, AGING: 4, NEWLY_DISCLOSED: 3}. After a full scan of babyagi-main, all 8 packages read NOT_APPLICABLE and vulnerability_age 'Not applicable', and the SBOM sheet's Age Bucket column shows NOT_APPLICABLE rather than unknown. Unit coverage asserts days=None with no disclosure -> NOT_APPLICABLE, days=None with a disclosure -> UNKNOWN, and that the dated buckets are unchanged.

gaps.title: 192 components were reported as RESOLVED with a non-SPDX licence string, and 3,409 more as unknown
gaps.problem: normalize_license returned its input unchanged for anything it did not recognise, and the caller then recorded license_resolution_status = RESOLVED_FROM_CANONICAL_REPORT with evidence_source = CANONICAL_REPORT. Every component in the corpus carries that status, so the resolver never consulted anything external.
gaps.reference_tool: SPDX License List; the value published as a resolved licence should be an SPDX identifier.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Normalise long-form and legacy spellings offline; never assert a resolution that did not happen.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Measured across all 23 corpus artifacts carrying license_evidence: 10,287 components, 3,409 unresolved (33.14%), concentrated in particular projects -- llama_index-main 95.0%, transformers-main 90.6%, peft-main 88.1%, diffusers-main 88.2%, dvpwa-master 88.9%, argip-platform 81.8% -- while wrongsecrets-master, WebGoat-master and BenchmarkJava-master were at 0%. Separately, 192 components carried a resolved value that is not SPDX-shaped, including 'GNU General Public License, version 2' (49), 'AGPLv3 License' (49), 'GNU General Public License, version 2 (GPL2)' (44), 'MIT/X11' (4) and 'SEE LICENSE IN COPYING.txt' (2).
gaps.actual_gap: PARTIALLY CLOSED, and the two halves are different problems. The 192 confident-wrong rows are fixed offline: long-form and legacy spellings now normalise to SPDX identifiers, a trailing parenthetical is stripped and the alias table retried so the next long form needs no new entry, and 'SEE LICENSE IN ...' returns UNRESOLVED_FILE_REFERENCE rather than being published as a licence -- it is a pointer, not an identifier, and it answers none of the questions a compliance reader asks. The 3,409 unresolved rows are NOT fixed, because a package whose manifest declares no licence cannot be resolved from the manifest: that needs an external source, which is a separate decision recorded here rather than taken silently. Note the confidently-wrong rows were the more damaging half: an unknown row is labelled as a gap so somebody looks at it, while a wrong licence with a RESOLVED status is quoted into a compliance answer with nothing to prompt a second look.
gaps.implementation_location: core/license_catalog.py (LICENSE_ALIASES, is_license_file_pointer, normalize_license); tests/test_v11_license_normalization.py
gaps.evidence: 30 tests in tests/test_v11_license_normalization.py, including that compound and parenthesised SPDX expressions ('(MIT AND CC-BY-3.0)', '(BSD-2-Clause OR MIT OR Apache-2.0)') pass through untouched and are not mangled by the trailing-parenthetical strip, and that 'HPND' -- a valid SPDX identifier my corpus heuristic over-flagged -- is not altered. GPL-2.0 is mapped to -only rather than -or-later because the long form states version 2 with no 'or later' qualifier; -or-later would be a redistribution decision this scan has no basis to make, and -only is the stricter reading.

gaps.title: Gap priority ignored severity and cost entirely, so 'fix first' had no defensible answer
gaps.problem: reports/gap_register.json ordered work by priority band and open-row count per root-cause class. That answers where weakness is concentrated and nothing about what to do first.
gaps.reference_tool: A prioritisation must combine importance with effort, or state which one it uses.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Rank by impact per unit of effort, with importance as a floor rather than as one input among several.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Added analysis/benchmark_root_cause_priority.py: every OPEN row is scored from register fields only -- priority weight, enterprise-essentiality, research relevance, evidence tier (a measured gap outranks an assumed one), regression risk, and domain concentration -- divided by the register's own cost field. Every component is printed with the output so a reader can disagree with a weight rather than reverse-engineer the arithmetic, and impact is asserted to equal the sum of its declared components so no term can hide.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED, and the substantive finding is the FIRST attempt at this, which was wrong. Ranking purely by value density produced: #1 G-045, a P3 'hand-maintained sink list' hygiene item at XS cost; #49 G-098, the BenchmarkJava recall 0.5512 baseline that carries the credibility of the entire accuracy claim; #71 G-083, CERT-In xBOM, the last unverified mandatory P0 standard. Impact-per-effort always favours small-and-trivial over large-and-important, which is the opposite of what was asked for, and the output looks perfectly reasonable unless you already know G-045 should not lead. The correction is a floor rather than a different formula: priority band is a HARD CONSTRAINT and density orders only WITHIN a band, so the two signals combine instead of one replacing the other -- priority is author judgement that no formula has access to, and density is informative about which of two equally-important rows to take first. The same starvation bug was then caught a second time at class level, where sorting batches by density alone let a class holding one cheap XS row lead the programme ahead of a class holding a P0; batches are now ordered by where their most important row falls in the programme order. Both rankings are published: the banded one as the programme order, the flat one explicitly labelled quick-wins. The model states in its own output that it is not a risk model and does not estimate the probability that a gap causes harm.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/benchmark_root_cause_priority.py (score_rows, banded_order, batched_order, render_md); tests/test_v11_root_cause_priority.py; reports/benchmark_root_cause_priority.{json,md}

gaps.title: AIVSS is absent, and a naive implementation would rest on roughly 3 of its 10 factors
gaps.problem: A peer red-team report (SATLAS 2026-09-22) scores AI findings on OWASP AIVSS, reporting 7.9/10 High with vector SV:C/VD:F/ASR:0.00. We have no AI scoring system at all: findings carry severity and risk_score, which are not the same thing.
gaps.reference_tool: OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System v0.8, aivss.owasp.org, co-published with AIUC-1; released 2026-03-19, ahead of RSAC 2026.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Extends CVSS v4.0 with ten agentic risk amplification factors, each scored 0.0 / 0.5 / 1.0: Autonomy, Tools, Language, Context, Non-Determinism, Opacity, Persistence, Identity, Multi-Agent, Self-Modification.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_OPEN, PARKED BY DECISION. Verified absent: no occurrence of 'aivss' in core/, scanner/, reporting/ or analysis/.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN. The specification is understood and citable: Factor_Sum is the sum of the ten factors, maximum 10.0; AARS = (10 - CVSS_Base) x (Factor_Sum / 10) x ThM, where ThM is the exploit-maturity multiplier defaulting to 0.97 (PoC); the final AIVSS = (CVSS_Base + AARS) x Mitigation_Factor, rounded to the nearest tenth, with Mitigation_Factor 1.0 for no/weak mitigation, 0.83 partial, 0.67 strong. PARKED because the design question is unresolved, not because the work is unclear. Two dependencies make a naive implementation actively harmful. First, AIVSS is conditional on a CVSS v4.0 base score, so emitting an AIVSS score asserts a CVSS v4.0 score we do not necessarily hold. Second, most of the ten factors are properties of a DEPLOYED agent -- autonomy level, identity, persistence, multi-agent -- which a static source analyser cannot observe. Tool scope is partly evidenced by the ABOM and non-determinism partly by configuration, but the remainder would have to be guessed. A score resting on roughly 3 of 10 factors, presented under an OWASP standard's name, is worse than no score: it looks comparable to the peer report's 7.9 when it is not computed the same way. The decision needed is whether to emit a score only when every factor is evidenced, or to emit per-factor status with an explicit UNASSESSED and no headline number. That representation should be chosen deliberately rather than defaulted into.
gaps.implementation_location: NOT STARTED. No file was created and nothing was written to the repository; verified by grep for 'aivss' across core/, scanner/, reporting/ and analysis/ returning zero.
gaps.evidence: Specification read from OWASP's published AIVSS v0.8 material (aivss.owasp.org and the v0.8 scoring publication): the ten factor names, the 0.0/0.5/1.0 per-factor scale, Factor_Sum maximum 10.0, the AARS and final-score formulas, the 0.97 PoC default for ThM, and the 0.67/0.83/1.0 Mitigation_Factor band. Absence of any AIVSS implementation verified by keyword search across production source: 0 occurrences.

gaps.title: The OWASP LLM rule engine cost 3.35x the core SAST phase and blocked the AI corpus rescan; now 2.75x faster with detection unchanged
gaps.problem: The AI-Benchmarks sweep could not complete llama_index-main or transformers-main at any budget tried (5,400s, 7,200s twice). Raising the budget was the tempting response and would have been the wrong one, because the cost is not in the scanner generally.
gaps.reference_tool: The scan's own PHASE START/END instrumentation, which the benchmark harness now parses (G-124).
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Attribute cost to a phase, then to a line, before deciding whether a budget is too small or the code is too slow.
gaps.current_behavior: PARTIALLY CLOSED. The measured slowdown is fixed and the fix is verified behaviour-preserving against the pre-change implementation over real repositories, not by a test asserting the new code returns what the new code returns. End-to-end on transformers-main at a 2,700s budget, the phase 'Scanning OWASP LLM security rules' fell from 1,648.0s to 599.0s -- 2.75x -- and the run no longer stalls mid-scan: it now reaches 'Generating PDF report', the final phase, having completed Advanced AI security rules (93.2s), Privacy data exposure (94.5s), ML-BOM (136.8s) and AI-BOM (210.2s). 'Scanning codebase' is unchanged at 514.0s against 492.3s, confirming the change is confined to the LLM engine rather than the pipeline.
gaps.actual_gap: PARTIALLY CLOSED, WITH THE REMAINING BLOCKER NOW A DIFFERENT PHASE. Four changes in scanner/llm_security.py, all required to be behaviour-preserving and all verified as such: (1) patterns compiled once through a memoised _rx rather than on every call, which was consulting re's internal cache 591,613 times over a 40-file sample; (2) character-by-character Unicode classification replaced by one str.translate against a table built from unicodedata itself, which was 6,363,199 unicodedata.category calls -- built from unicodedata rather than hardcoded because a hardcoded Cf list is a hand transcription that goes stale against a Unicode version bump, the same defect class as the hand-maintained ATLAS catalogue that G-131 had to remove; (3) transforms that cannot change their input are skipped, each guarded by a C-level scan for its own trigger character, and NFKC is skipped for ASCII input where it is the identity; (4) the format-character strip stays LAST because decoding can PRODUCE a format character -- \u00ad yields SOFT HYPHEN and %EF%BB%BF yields U+FEFF, both category Cf -- so a strip running earlier would silently change detection. A fifth idea was tried and REVERTED: one alternation over all 155 patterns of the 38 pattern-only rules, searched once per line as a superset gate. It was correct but SLOWER, because Python's re optimises a single pattern's literal prefix and a 155-way alternation has none, so it tried every alternative at every position. What remains is structural rather than incidental: re.Pattern.search still runs about 1,153,215 times over 40 files, because every one of 171 patterns is tried against every line. Further gains need the engine restructured, not tuned, and that is a larger change deserving its own validation rather than being folded into a verified one. NOT CLOSED: the full corpus rescan this was meant to enable has not happened; transformers-main now stalls in PDF report generation rather than in detection.

gaps.title: 37% of LLM findings discarded the pattern that detected them, and the leak was invisible by construction
gaps.problem: Every LLM finding carries a detection_note naming the pattern that fired. For most findings it named nothing at all.
gaps.reference_tool: Not a reference-tool gap. Found by a before/after differential over real repositories, which is the only thing that could surface it.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Evidence is derived from the record of the specific match, never from a variable left over from an earlier loop.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. scanner/llm_security.py builds detection_note as f'{title} matched pattern: {matched_pattern}' when matched_pattern is set and a generic sentence when it is not. The pattern was stored per match at the line_matches append and never read; the note instead read the bare loop variable in the emit loop. That variable is reset to None at the top of EVERY rule iteration, and all 40 rules are evaluated for every line whether or not they match, so by emit time it held whatever the last rule in LLM_RULES happened to leave behind -- almost always None.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. The consequence is worse than a cross-rule annotation error, which is how it first looked. Because the reset happens per rule rather than per line, EVERY finding that matched through an explicit pattern lost its attribution, not just lines where two rules both matched. Measured: 241 of 651 findings (37%) across 300 real files of the AI Benchmarks corpus carried the generic note where a specific pattern was available, and on the 90-file peft-main and transformers-main subset 115 of 115 such findings were generic -- a 100% loss on that path. The lost values were the specificity aliases, the LLM01 additional patterns, the PI category ids and the two markers LLM02_SENSITIVE_EVIDENCE and PI-006_SPLIT_PAYLOAD, so the note never once reported which rule path had fired. FIXED by reading match.get('matched_pattern') in the emit loop, which is where the correct value had always been stored. The value was also previously dead data: nothing in the repository read it.
gaps.implementation_location: scanner/llm_security.py (emit loop over line_matches); tests/test_v11_llm_matched_pattern_provenance.py
gaps.evidence: Before the fix, on a fixture whose only finding matches a specificity alias: 'LLM Sensitive Information Disclosure matched a compiled rule pattern'. After: 'LLM Sensitive Information Disclosure matched pattern: return.*token'. Corpus counts from the before/after differential over 300 files: 241 of 651 findings changed their detection_note and nothing else changed. Re-running the corpus invariants against the pre-change snapshot gives 115 of 115 findings generic on the peft-main and transformers-main first-30-files subset. tests/test_v11_llm_matched_pattern_provenance.py pins both directions: an alias match must name its alias, and a combined-pattern match must still report the generic note, so a fix that always interpolated something cannot pass. It also asserts the invariant over real repository files rather than fixtures, which is where a third marker class surfaced: PI-005 is appended from the obfuscation_detected flag and is therefore absent from _V11_PI_PATTERNS, so deriving the permitted ids from that table alone rejected legitimate attribution.
