gaps.title: merge() silently deleted the record of every scan timeout, destroying the evidence of what blocked each project
gaps.problem: The benchmark harness's merge() was documented LOSSLESS and was lossy in the only sense that mattered.
gaps.reference_tool: Not a reference-tool gap. A measurement harness whose own summary cannot be trusted is the defect.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: A superseding record carries the history of what it superseded; a failure is never erased by a later success.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py merge() loaded the existing sweep file into a dict keyed by project and let each fresh entry overwrite the old one. No project name was ever dropped, which is exactly what the docstring promised and exactly as far as the implementation went. A fresh entry, however, carries none of the fields that make a failure diagnosable: returncode, error, stdout_tail, stderr_tail, phase_seconds, phases_completed, timeout_seconds, timed_out, overshoot_seconds, hung_in_phase and seconds. All of that was destroyed on replacement. There was no test for merge() at any point, so a docstring asserting a property sat next to an implementation that did not have it.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. This was not hypothetical and not harmless. transformers-main timed out at a 2,700s budget after 1,648.0s in the OWASP LLM phase and wrote its clean_report.json before dying in PDF generation. The next run found that artifact, re-derived it, and overwrote the timeout record with an rc=0 row carrying none of the diagnostic. The sweep file then asserted that transformers-main had never failed to scan, and the single record explaining where the 1,648s had gone was deleted by the very run that resolved the stall. FIXED: a recorded failure superseded by a non-failure is carried forward under prior_attempts, deduplicated by content because merge() is called once per project with accumulated results and would otherwise re-append a project's own history on every iteration, while genuinely distinct failures still accumulate. Verified by running the old and new implementations side by side on the real transformers-main timeout record: old yields a 6-key row with the evidence DESTROYED, new yields the row with prior_attempts intact including hung_in_phase 'Generating PDF report'. The related claim is closed too: a re-derived entry carried returncode 0 with seconds 0 and nothing distinguishing it from a completed scan of the current build, so scanned_this_run is now set explicitly to False on re-derivation and True on a real scan -- returncode 0 in this harness means an artifact exists and parses, which is not a claim that this build was scanned.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (merge, _FAILURE_EVIDENCE, _is_failed_attempt, _failure_evidence, _same_evidence, scan_one and the re-derivation branch); tests/test_v11_benchmark_merge_evidence.py
gaps.evidence: Old merge on the real record: row keys ['findings_len','project','returncode','scanned_this_run','seconds'] -- prior_attempts absent, evidence DESTROYED. New merge on the same input: prior_attempts present and prior_attempts[0]['hung_in_phase'] == 'Generating PDF report'. Nine tests cover: the timeout's phase, overshoot, timings and stderr surviving supersession; the fresh row still reporting current numbers; history not duplicating across three successive merges; two distinct failures accumulating to two records; project names still never dropped; a fresh failure still replacing the old record; a missing sweep file not being an error; and both directions of scanned_this_run.

gaps.how_reference_does_it: A flag that promises to skip work must gate the work, and must say so in --help.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. main.py declared --no-pdf at line 2526 with no help text and referenced it nowhere in the file. --no-excel, on the adjacent line, was honoured. The PDF block at main.py:4912-4943 -- the main report and the executive report -- sat outside any guard. The only no_pdf reference in that region was at line 4873, and it guarded only a _step() label, not the rendering.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED. Verified by execution rather than by reading source, because a flag that parses cleanly and does nothing is indistinguishable from working code by inspection. A probe scan of a small directory with --no-pdf still wrote Security_Report.pdf at 64,468 bytes and Security_Executive_Report.pdf at 56,867 bytes. The consequence was concrete rather than cosmetic: both large AI-corpus projects were timing out in 'Generating PDF report', which was the only thing between them and a quotable artifact. llama_index-main spent 770.4s of a 3,600s budget on detection phases -- ML-BOM 205.1s, OWASP LLM 184.2s, AI-BOM 143.8s, codebase 118.0s, secrets 75.9s, IOC 43.4s -- and roughly 2,800s rendering a document the benchmark harness never reads, because it summarises from clean_report.json, written at main.py:4868 before that block. The corpus harness now passes --no-pdf and records pdfs_not_rendered plus a rendering_note in the sweep file rather than leaving the omission implicit. The comment already in main.py below that block named the hazard exactly: a reader cannot tell a report with no PDF from one where none was asked for, and the 'asked for' path was dead.

After: the same command produces zero PDFs and still writes clean_report.json, Security_CycloneDX.json, Security_SPDX.spdx.json and Scan_Performance.json; a default run still produces both PDFs. gaps.title: The corpus harness never recomputed staleness for carried-forward rows, and the rendered markdown never distinguished them either
gaps.problem: Rows merged from a previous sweep kept whatever stale flag they had, or none at all, and a missing flag was read as fresh.
gaps.reference_tool: The module's own artifact_staleness(), which is correct; it was simply not called for rows the run had not touched.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: Every reported aggregate is recomputed from source state at report time, never carried forward from a previous report.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_CLOSED. Staleness was computed only inside the per-target loop, for the project in the current invocation. Rows carried forward by merge() retained the stale value from whenever they last ran, or no key at all. The reporting filter was `fresh = [r for r in ok if not r.get("stale")]`, and None is falsy.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_CLOSED, AND IT CORRUPTED A HEADLINE NUMBER. Measured directly: the transformers-main artifact was 5.69 hours older than main.py, so it was stale by the harness's own rule, yet its sweep row carried stale=None and was counted in 'projects scanned cleanly: 2 / 9' and folded into the 4,193 findings reported as 'current build only'. The harness was asserting that a project described the current build when it demonstrably did not -- the same absence-read-as-evidence inversion as G-125 and G-137, in the component that produces the numbers people quote. It triggers on every partial run: `--only llama_index` recomputed that one flag and left the other eight untouched, so a run that improves one project can leave the others quietly overstating their currency with no visible change in the output. FIXED in three parts: refresh_staleness() recomputes the flag from the artifact on disk for every row not scanned in this run, called after each merge and once more before the summary; a row with no artifact gets stale=None explicitly so unknown is recorded as unknown; and the filter requires `stale is False`, with a separate 'currency never established' bucket that is named in the summary and excluded from the current-build totals. A scan completing in this run sets stale False, which is what makes that value mean 'known current' rather than 'not known to be old'. After the fix the harness honestly reports 0 of 9 projects describing the current build and 9 stale, where it previously claimed 2 of 9. THE FIX WAS INCOMPLETE ON FIRST PASS, AND THE REMAINDER WAS FOUND BY ASKING WHAT ELSE READS THESE ROWS. Fixing the console summary left the RENDERED markdown untouched, and the markdown is the document a person actually reads. It had no staleness column, so a row built from an artifact 5.69 hours older than main.py rendered identically to a current one; its Severity mix, Top rules and AI mapping engagement tables all aggregated over the unfiltered ok, silently blending stale and current findings into single counts; and the only section naming non-current rows keyed on returncode, which a stale artifact satisfies. A reader of the .md could not tell that any of it described an older build. Now: a currency column reading current / stale / unverified (three values, because currency never established is not the same claim as known to be old), every aggregate computed over stale is False rows, a section naming the excluded rows with their reasons, and each aggregate caption stating its population. Ten tests assert on the rendered markdown rather than on the source, since the defect is that the output did not distinguish the rows and checking the code would have passed while the document stayed wrong. This is the shape of hazard 6 in AGENTS.md -- aggregates disagreeing with the rows beneath them -- except here the aggregate was not merely stale, it was undiscriminated.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (refresh_staleness, the fresh/stale/unverified filters, the summary line); tests/test_v11_benchmark_staleness_forwarding.py; the rendered markdown: currency column, currency-scoped aggregates, excluded-rows section in write_reports; tests/test_v11_sweep_markdown_currency.py
gaps.evidence: Measured before the fix: transformers-main artifact mtime 5.69h older than main.py, sweep row stale=None, counted in 'projects scanned cleanly: 2 / 9' and in the 4,193 'current build only' findings. Measured after: 'projects scanned cleanly: 0 / 9', 'from a stale artifact: 9', 'currency never established: 0', with all nine named and 11,115 stale findings over 4,268 kloc explicitly excluded from the totals. Eight tests, including that a carried-forward row is recomputed, that a missing artifact yields None rather than an absent key, that a row scanned this run is fresh by construction, and that every row is refreshed rather than only the named one. NOTE ON A TEST THAT WAS WEAKER THAN ITS MESSAGE: the static assertion originally searched only inside ast.BoolOp for `not r.get("stale")`, and reported the pre-fix file as clean -- because the original defect is a comprehension condition, a bare ast.UnaryOp with no BoolOp around it. Corrected to match any UnaryOp(Not), after which the pre-fix file is detected. A guard that passed against the exact code it exists to catch is worse than no guard.

gaps.title: ML-BOM generation scales superlinearly on large Python projects, 27x worse than linear at 3.8x the code
gaps.problem: The ML-BOM framework/model inventory phase is the slowest phase on the largest project in the corpus, and it is not merely proportional to size.
gaps.reference_tool: The same phase on a smaller project in the same corpus, same build, same machine.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: A phase's cost should be proportional to the input it processes.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_OPEN. Measured within one sweep run, same build, same host. llama_index-main at 471 kloc: 'Generating ML-BOM framework/model inventory' 205.1s in one run and 192.33s in another. transformers-main at 1,788 kloc: 3,879.1s. The code is 3.8x larger and the phase is 19-20x slower. Linear scaling would predict about 780s.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN, AND IT IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT. transformers-main has now never completed a scan. It carries 4,173 findings, 1,788 kloc, 142+ attack paths and the largest artifact in the corpus, and ML-BOM is the phase that consumes the budget before anything else gets a look in. The superlinearity is the finding, not the absolute time: a linear phase would have cost ~780s and left ample room. NOT CLOSED and not attempted here -- the cause is not yet attributed to a line, and attributing it needs instrumentation inside the ML-BOM generator rather than the phase timings the harness already captures. What is known is that it is not the OWASP LLM engine any more: that work was done in G-134, and the same phase on llama_index is 205s. Two measurements to take next, in order of value: ML-BOM wall time against kloc across all nine projects, which would give a scaling curve rather than two points; and a cProfile of the ML-BOM generator on transformers, which is where the attribution belongs. Note that cProfile exaggerates changes that alter call count, so its verdict here should be confirmed by isolated per-process timing before anything is optimised on the strength of it.
gaps.implementation_location: main.py (the ML-BOM generation phase); the framework/model inventory generator it calls
gaps.evidence: Same sweep, same build: transformers-main phase breakdown gives ML-BOM 3,879.1s, Scanning OWASP LLM security rules 1,696.8s, Scanning codebase 495.4s, AI-BOM 281.6s, Advanced AI security rules 273.4s, ABOM 229.2s; STALLED IN Scanning Secret Intelligence; rc=-9 after 7,196s. llama_index-main (471 kloc) in the same sweep: ML-BOM 192.33s, slowest phase. kloc ratio 3.8x, ML-BOM ratio 20.2x. 'Scanning codebase' is the control: 495.4s against 514.0s in an earlier standalone run, i.e. flat, so the inflation is specific to ML-BOM rather than uniform host slowdown across the pipeline.

gaps.title: The harness timeout is enforced by the supervising process, so it overshot 100% under host memory pressure
gaps.problem: A 3,600s budget produced a 7,196s run.
gaps.reference_tool: The same budget earlier in the day, on the same harness, overshoot 0s and 1s.
gaps.how_reference_does_it: A deadline enforced by a process that can itself be starved is not a deadline.
gaps.current_behavior: MEASURED_OPEN. analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py enforces the per-project budget with proc.communicate(timeout=timeout) in the harness process. On timeout it calls _kill_tree, which is bounded: taskkill with timeout=120 and proc.wait(timeout=60), so at most ~180s, followed by a communicate(timeout=120) capture with its own cap. The worst-case overshoot those paths can produce is therefore roughly 300s. A 3,596s overshoot is not reachable from them.
gaps.actual_gap: MEASURED_OPEN. transformers-main, the ninth of nine consecutive scans on a 19.8 GB host, ran 7,196s against a 3,600s budget and reported the 3,596s overshoot explicitly. Since the kill path cannot account for it, the budget itself did not fire on time: the supervising process was not scheduled to notice its own deadline. The same host had 4.8 GB free afterwards, and transformers is the largest target with the largest artifact, so memory exhaustion during the ninth consecutive scan is the plausible cause -- but it is not proven, and the honest position is that the mechanism by which the deadline was missed is not established. What IS established is the consequence for interpretation: a timeout in this harness is a lower bound on runtime, never an upper bound, so 'the project was slow' cannot be distinguished from 'the host ran out of memory' using this harness alone. That is why G-140 leans on a control -- Scanning codebase at 495.4s, flat against 514.0s -- rather than on the raw ML-BOM figure. NOT CLOSED: the fix is not obvious. Enforcing the deadline from outside the starved process (a watchdog, or a job-level deadline) is a design change, and reducing peak memory is G-140's work. Recorded because the next person to see a large overshoot will otherwise assume the kill path regressed, and today it demonstrably did not.
gaps.implementation_location: analysis/compare_ai_benchmarks.py (scan_one timeout handling, _kill_tree at line 201)
gaps.evidence: transformers-main: 'rc=-9 after 7196s TIMEOUT after 3600s (ran 7196s, overshoot 3596s)'. _kill_tree bounds: taskkill timeout=120, proc.wait(timeout=60), then communicate(timeout=120) -- so ~300s maximum reachable overshoot, against 3,596s observed. Earlier same-day runs of the same harness on the same host reported overshoot 0s (transformers at 2,700s and 4,500s budgets) and 1s (llama_index at 3,600s), so the kill path was behaving correctly immediately before this run. Host memory after the sweep: 4.8 GB free of 19.8 GB total.

not_proposed.reason: Crosswalk holds 21 DSGAI and 10 AST entries, but a case-insensitive repo-wide search finds zero references to `DSGAI` or `AST0#`, no detector emits them and no report surface renders them. Catalogue data with no consumer would be data for its own sake; re-proposed only alongside a detector or a mapping that consumes it.

not_proposed.item: Cross-function propagation of operator-controlled sources (os.getenv, os.environ, sys.argv, input)
not_proposed.reason: The threat model this product scores is untrusted *network* input reaching a dangerous sink (ground truth `scoping_rules.in_scope`: "a demonstrable untrusted source"). Intra-procedural handling of these tokens is unchanged - they still taint inside the function that reads them, which is pre-G-035 baseline behaviour and is protected. What is withheld is only the new same-file call-seeding step. The first implementation of G-035 seeded unconditionally; measured on this corpus that produced three command-injection findings inside a generic CLI runner via `run_cmd(f'cd "{SANDBOX_DIR}" && {engine} build ...')` where SANDBOX_DIR came from `os.getenv`, plus a violation of negative control NC-03 (1/6 -> back to 0/6). Reported as command injection when an operator's own environment variable reaches a shell in their own tool is a false positive, not a finding. Re-proposed only alongside a separate trust-tier concept where env/CLI taint is reported with an explicit operator-controlled provenance label rather than as an attacker source.

not_proposed.item: Exclude `benchmark_synthetic` findings from the primary count
not_proposed.reason: 218 findings on the Juice Shop corpus carry analysis_scope=benchmark_synthetic, and the console wording '0 synthetic findings excluded' was misleading, so exclusion looked like the obvious fix. It is not safe: the one synthetic finding that matches ground truth is the JWT_TOKEN_SIGNATURE at test/server/verify.unit.test.ts, which is itself marked benchmark_synthetic. Withholding synthetic findings would drop challenge coverage from 13/116 to 12/116 and delete a declared-intentional match in order to make a count look cleaner. The message was changed instead to report marked and excluded counts separately, which fixes the ambiguity without moving a benchmark number.

not_proposed.item: Add i18n/locale, data/static and test paths to `_skip()` or to a blanket secret-rule allowlist
not_proposed.reason: The obvious implementation of G-048 would exclude whole files from scanning. Measured against the ground truth that would be destructive: 8 of the 10 DIRECT_CHALLENGE_KEY_EVIDENCE matches live in config/fbctf.yml and the JWT match lives in a test file, so a path-based file skip or a test/ allowlist would remove real declared-intentional coverage. Only CONFIG_CONTEXTUAL_CREDENTIAL - the specific key/value misinterpretation - is withheld, and only inside locale bundles and seed datasets; known-signature, PEM, URI, JWT and entropy detection still run there, pinned by a test that puts a PEM inside an i18n catalogue and expects it to be reported.
